description: We are participating for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, focusing on spatial mapping, autonomous navigation, and AI integration for the Martian Map challenge. This is a closed team of two, and we are not currently accepting new members. Good luck to everyone participating!
summary: Marswalk is a route and map planner for a crew-and-rover pair exploring the boxwork terrain on Mount Sharp, Gale Crater. A crew on Mars needs a map at walking scale: where an astronaut can walk, where a rover can drive, and where they meet. Using real HiRISE terrain data, Marswalk builds a separate terrain-cost map for each agent, plans a route for each, picks three science stops, checks that everyone stays inside a 400 m abort radius, and estimates the radiation dose of the whole excursion. The result is shown on a tablet-style page with map layers, a 3D terrain view, a route profile, a radiation panel with a solar-storm what-if, and a simulated rover-camera view. On our real test window the astronaut route is 565 m long with a steepest slope of 17.6° and a dose of 7.9 µGy over 54 minutes. Every number is labelled as sourced, derived, assumed or simulated, so a crew can see what to trust.
details:
Challenge: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map.

How it meets the challenge. The challenge asks for a layered, integrated view that combines data from multiple NASA science missions to help a human explorer plan a Marswalk. Marswalk layers data from two NASA missions on one map: elevation and imagery from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's HiRISE camera (slope, rocks, ridges, hollows, 3D terrain) and surface radiation measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument on the Mars Science Laboratory mission (dose estimate). On top of that it adds the planning step a crew needs: routes for an astronaut and a rover, science stops at the boxwork (a honeycomb of raised ridges and hollows, with the dense part of it called the "lattice zone" below), an abort radius and a dose check.

What it does. For a 500 x 500 m window of Mount Sharp (Gale Crater), Marswalk builds one terrain-cost map for an astronaut on foot and one for a rover, plans a route for each, and reports the result. The astronaut walks slopes up to 25 degrees and may cross ridges at a cost. The rover drives slopes up to 15 degrees and never crosses ridges, so it goes to the edge of the lattice, then as close to the other stops as it can get, and returns to the habitat. The tool reports route length, time, steepest slope, the farthest distance from the habitat against a 400 m abort radius, and the radiation dose of the excursion against a limit.

How it works. (1) It loads a HiRISE elevation model (DTM) and the matching orthoimage. (2) The DTM gives slope, rocks and route heights. It cannot resolve the boxwork lattice, so ridges, hollows and the lattice zone come from the orthoimage brightness, a proxy that is labelled as such. (3) It builds a cost grid per agent and runs A* with no corner-cutting. (4) A rule-based step picks the habitat and three stops: the lattice margin, the lattice interior and the bluff contact. (5) A report step writes every number with a label. (6) The rover cost grid is exported as a Nav2 map and tested in ROS 2 Nav2. (7) A single-file tablet page shows everything.

Results on the real window. Astronaut: 565 m, steepest slope 17.6 degrees, 9.4 min of walking, 54 min including 15 min at each stop, dose 7.9 microGy against a 50 microGy limit, farthest point 232 m from the habitat (inside the 400 m abort radius). Rover: 605 m, steepest slope 14.2 degrees, 20 min, farthest point 225 m from the habitat, returns to base.

Benefits. A crew gets one place to see where each agent can go, how far from the habitat it is, and how much radiation the plan costs, before anyone leaves. A what-if slider shows how a solar particle event would change the verdict.

Intended impact. Surface crews will need planning at walking scale, where orbital maps and rover autonomy meet. Marswalk shows that this can be built from public HiRISE data and runs in a browser. The same pipeline can run on any HiRISE terrain window, so a crew could plan any site. Next steps: more sites, live re-planning, real radiation time series, and a crew in the loop.

What is creative. One site is planned for two different agents that share a base and a rendezvous. Every number carries a label (sourced, derived, assumed or simulated), so the crew can see what to trust. The tablet shows the dose against a budget and lets the user stress-test it with a solar-storm slider.

Factors we considered. Slope limits for each agent, ridges and soft hollows, rocks, the abort radius, time at each stop, and radiation dose. We also considered how honest the data is: the lattice comes from image brightness, not elevation, and the rover battery and rover-camera view are simulated.

Limits. Ridges and hollows come from image brightness, not elevation. Stops follow simple rules. Speeds, slope limits, dwell time, the 400 m abort radius and the 50 microGy limit are our assumptions. The solar-storm multiplier is a hypothetical stress test.

Tools. Python, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, rasterio, three.js for the 3D view, plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the tablet page, ROS 2 Jazzy with Nav2 and RViz2 for the planner test, git and GitHub Pages for hosting.

Code and map pack: https://github.com/gab-lap/marswalk-martian-map

Some code in this repository was written with the help of Claude (Anthropic) and Gemini (Google), primarily the frontend. A UI mockup generated with AI was used as a visual reference starting point when designing the tablet page; the page in `tablet/` is a separate implementation. All results shown were produced by running the code; all the AI-written text and code were reviewed by the team. No NASA logos or mission identifiers appear in generated content.
